cards.explanation: The answer is carry on business and make a profit. The planners say they'll spend a year in some city, carry on business and make a profit (James 4:13). Notice what's missing, friends: not one word about asking the Lord first. A year of business, all mapped out, and nobody checked who owns the calendar.

The answer is False. James says the exact opposite: "You do not even know what will happen tomorrow!" (James 4:14). The planners sound sure about a whole year, but they can't see past the next sunrise. I know that feeling, friends, because I've had tomorrow flip on me without warning.

The answer is a mist that soon vanishes. James says, "You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes." (James 4:14). A mist shows up, hangs around a bit and is gone. Short, quiet and over before you can set a timer.

The answer is willing. James says they ought to say, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that." (James 4:15). Plans aren't banned, friends. He just wants the Lord in them. Make the plan, hold it loosely and let Him have the last word.

The answer is evil, and James doesn't soften it: "All such boasting is evil." (James 4:16). Boasting in proud intentions means acting like tomorrow belongs to you. That's a strong word, friends, and he means it.

The answer is that they are guilty of sin. James says, "Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin." (James 4:17). It isn't only about doing wrong things. Knowing the good thing and skipping it counts too. That one makes me stop and think.

The answer is weep. James says, "…weep and wail over the misery to come upon you." (James 5:1). He's talking to the rich, and he doesn't start with a pat on the back. Misery is coming, friends, and he tells them to weep over it.

The answer is that moths have eaten them. James says, "Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes." (James 5:2). Fine clothes in the closet, and moths made lunch of them. I think that's a hard way to find out what stored-up stuff is worth.
The answer is False. James says, "Your gold and silver are corroded." (James 5:3). Nothing shiny about it, friends. Treasure sitting in storage ends up looking like the bottom of a very old pan.

The answer is that it will testify against them. James says, "Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire." (James 5:3). The rust itself speaks up like a witness. A pile of treasure left sitting has a lot to say.

The answer is their wages. James says, "…the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields…" (James 5:4). The workers mowed the fields, and their wages were withheld, friends. I think that stings.

The answer is True. James says, "The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts." (James 5:4). The harvesters may have felt unheard, but their cries got through. I take comfort, friends, that He hears every one.

The answer is luxury. James says, "You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence." (James 5:5). Comfort and indulgence were the daily menu. That's a sharp contrast with the harvesters waiting on their pay.

The answer is False. James says the righteous "…did not resist you." (James 5:6). They didn't fight back against those who condemned and murdered them. I think this is a heavy verse, friends, and it deserves a quiet moment.
